Content:
Hi there,

I’m really excited about the new ROG Xbox Ally, but I’ve run into a question that no one seems to have a clear answer to. Now that the system is officially out, I’m hoping someone can help clarify this.

Here’s my situation: I have two Xbox consoles at home, a Series X that I use, and a Series S that my wife plays on. To ensure she can access all the games I own, I’ve set the Series S as my home console. I play on the Series X, which works because the games are tied to my profile as well.

When I head up into the mountains for the weekend, where I have no internet signal, I sometimes bring my Series X. Unfortunately, most of my games won’t launch offline because the system needs to verify ownership online. If I bring the Series S instead (with games updated and ready), offline play works fine because games are tied to my home console. But I’m really hoping the Xbox Ally can offer a more portable solution without needing to haul a full console.

So here’s my question: How well does the ROG Xbox Ally work offline? Does it require being set as my home console to play downloaded games without a connection?

What I’m hoping for is a way to use the Ally offline without needing to designate it as my home console, and still be able to play my owned games (excluding online-only titles like ESO or Call of Duty Multiplayer, of course). Alternatively, if Microsoft now allows two home consoles, that would solve the issue as well.

Have you tested this scenario? If not, is it something you could look into and share your findings? I think this is a real-world concern that hasn’t been addressed yet, and it’s important for those of us who game in offline environments.

Author: @originalfate4788
Content:
The days of subsidized consoles are over. As early as 2021, less than a year after its release, Sony announced the PS5 was no longer selling at a loss. While Xbox never made a similar announcement, it stands to reason they likely cleared that hurdle sometime after. 

While a price drop wasn’t going to follow anytime soon, year 3-4 (2024/25) is usually when it would have happened. It didn’t. 

Yeah sure, tariffs are a thing, and so is greed, but the more likely culprit to maintain profitability is the gaming market in general. More console owners are buying less games. Less games being sold (both 1st and 3rd party) the tighter the margins. This is why you can now expect once exclusive Sony games to hit PC more often and at a faster cadence. 

I fully expect both new home consoles to start at $899, and assuming both do a handheld, around $699, if not more. 

Lastly, Steam Deck can get away with those prices for 2 reasons. Sold directly from Steam, not in stores, and a fully digital storefront for gaming which is the default loadout.

The new OS on the Steam Deck is pretty good, no question better than WIndows 11 alone, and is better to navigate games.  I don't like Microsoft's marketing here. Yep, after owning a Steam Deck from launch, after 3 years, 100% modded (case, OLED, Hall sticks, etc), I'm going to be selling it soon and moving to a Windows based device. Author: @Alovon
Content:
Waiting for Panther Lake or a NV HH at this point. The problem I have with my ROG Ally is games that are too heavy even at 720p. (Aka most UE5 games). Which the problem with those are an architectural design issue with AMD stripping Cache amounts so much in their APUs aside Strix Halo that Switch 2 has more L1 Cache than both the L0 and L1 of the SERIES S COMBINED. Much less the actual AMD HH APUs.

Meanwhile NVIDIA besides giving their GPUs sufficient cache and extra width to keep more tasks in-flight. Intel is doubling down on that ideology with Panther Lake and putting 16MB of L2 cache, in a 12Core GPU! 

And well, we know how much 16MB of slower L3 can help a “12 Core” GPU as we have the 12CU RX6400. Which despite being lower clocked, 1.5gens older, and even slower GDDR now in some cases, STILL dogwalks the 12CU and even 16CU 890M.

And Xe3 in Panther Lake has NVIDIA style  128 Shaders per Core so it can also keep more tasks in-flight before cycling to Cache or RAM just like the Switch 2’s notable above-tier GPU

Which the Cache and Width points are doubly important for UE5 games as Nanite in particular heavily stresses both of those, and AMD’s lack of Infinity Cache in their APUs causes the smaller ones to immediately dump out into RAM rather than stay in cache, and double slow by having fewer tasks in flight and having to cycle tasks in and out of the shaders more often

Author: @FlyHighorFlyHome
Content:
Microsoft's Xbox product team are going to have to take the L on this one for not revealing their long term roadmap. 

But with the release of the FSE and why the initial news of this was big for me is when you read between the lines.

Frankly I don't see Microsoft releasing another console like we've seen in the past. 

Instead, I think we're going to start seeing Xbox branded portable gaming PCs (like the ally x) sprouting up. 

I think Microsoft's next "console" will instead be an eGPU that hooks up to a TV that all of these Xbox branded portables will then be certified against for that consistent AAA gaming experience people look for. 

Whether the whole existing catalog makes its way over is left to be seen but given Microsoft does the whole "agile" release method, this is clearly a good MVP and the path forward for Microsoft is some sort of Nintendo/Valve like portable that can go onto a TV?

I don't know, either way this is a really exciting space right now and I expect big news over the next year about what the future really holds.

Is it an Xbox?  Here is the real answer:

Microsoft is changing the Xbox OS to a windows based one for the next generation Xbox.  Doing this will allow them to have the freedom of windows when it comes to launchers like Steam, Xbox,, PlayStation, pc gaming and emulators but will not run native Xbox (early xb1, 360 and earlier) games, a trade-off most actual Xbox gamers would happily make.

For those that really want those games, Microsoft has stated they would restore this compatibility via emulation for the next gen console and this Xbox ally x can stream from an existing series console (much like the PlayStation Portal does) or the cloud.

So to answer the question, this is the first of the new Xbox windows hybrid OS consoles so that makes it an Xbox IMO

Author: @BAMozzy69
Content:
Xbox 'stopped' being JUST their Console around a decade ago - when they merged Xbox as a small separate part of MS into the full MS ecosystem. That meant they released EVERY game Day/Date on PC, built Xbox into Windows and created Play Anywhere and Game Pass. Of course there are a LOT of 3rd Party Published games that didn't support Play Anywhere or Game Pass and of course a lot of historical releases too never had PC releases. 

Microsoft's 'Gaming' brand is Xbox - whether you play on their Console, Cloud or 'their' ecosystem on PC (Game Pass, Play Anywhere, Windows store games) - but PC also is a Multi-platform device (not a Single Platform like Console) so has Steam, Epic etc Platforms too. When you get a 'Play Anywhere' game, its NOT the Steam or Epic platform, its the Windows/Xbox Platform. 

Of course its a PC and MS can't force Publishers/Devs to retroactively provide PC versions (especially not if they only released on Steam or Epic on PC) of their Console releases so their is a 'compromise'. You have Play Anywhere and/or Game Pass to play Natively, but you can stream some of your owned games and/or Remote Play from your cconsole so effectively can play 'every' Xbox game you own just not all of them natively - but as its using the Xbox FSE and that links to Game Pass and MS store directly, its an 'Xbox' as its set-up to run in the Xbox Ecosystem primarily - but yes you can also access Steam via an App, like accessing Netflix on your Console. 

At least that's how MS are approaching it - the Xbox Console was only brought to market so MS and others could bring their 'PC' games to a more mainstream market and make DirectX important for Game Developers who had to use it for both Windows and now their Console games. 25yrs Later and you now have 'affordable' Gaming PC's able to run the latest games at 'Console' like settings. But Windows, Xbox, DirectX, Game Pass etc are ALL MS owned so all customers are MS customers in their ecosystem - unlike the 360 era in particular, MS are not treating their Windows gamers as 2nd class Gamers, unworthy to get MS games Day/date if at all, but instead trying to 'merge' their Gamers into one Ecosystem with 'different' ways to access to suit different budgets and/or preferences.

The cheapest entry point is via Cloud - lowest Quality visuals and Library, but available on so many different devices that you already own something to play on. 
Next tier is the Consoles - Series S is cheap but doesn't offer the best Graphics or Performance, but does have a BIG Library and lots of choice
Top Tier is the PC - Not only do you get MS releases Day/date, you get Game Pass and streaming options, the biggest Library because its not locked to 'just' Microsoft/Xbox and the option to spec it how you choose for the best Graphics/Performance  for your budget, and can be upgraded to.

Point is 'Xbox' itself stopped being JUST the Console but the entire 'Gaming' branch of Microsoft on ANY device (including iOS/Android) their customers can use to access their 'gaming' ecosystem. You play on Cloud, you are playing on Series Consoles built into servers, play on PC via Game Pass (native or streaming) or Windows Store/play anywhere, its still the Xbox ecosystem - but play on Steam or Epic on your PC, that's not the Xbox/Microsoft ecosystem/platform. MS has an 'Xbox' platform on PC because that's MS's Gaming Brand and built into Windows too. Just because 'PC' gamers tend to choose Steam and Epic doesn't mean that 'Xbox' doesn't have a Platform too on PC...
